questions.question: When is a partial index a good idea?

faithfulness.rationale: All claims are directly supported: excluding common values reduces index size and update work; stable distributions are best; unbilled-orders and partial unique-index use cases are described; query conditions must imply the predicate in recognizable form; and partial indexes require care with often minimal advantage.

questions.answer:
A partial index can be a good idea when it excludes common values that queries are unlikely to search by, reducing index size and speeding up queries that do use it and many table updates. This works best when the data distribution is stable, since the common values must be predetermined. [P1]

It can also help when typical queries focus on a small subset of rows, such as unbilled orders, or when you want a unique constraint to apply only to rows matching a predicate. [P1][P2][P3]

The query conditions must imply the index predicate in a form PostgreSQL can recognize. Partial indexes require care, and their advantage over regular indexes is often minimal. [P2][P3]

questions.question: What are the practical differences between the json and jsonb types?
